CLOSE CORPORATION — FORMATION INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

CLOSE CORPORATION ELECTION AND PURPOSE DECLARATION
The name of the corporation is Acme, Inc. Acme, Inc. elects to be governed by the close corporation provisions of California's General Corporation Law (Cal. Corp. Code § 158 et seq.). All of Acme, Inc.'s issued shares of all classes shall be held of record by not more than 35 persons. This corporation is a close corporation. Acme, Inc. is authorized to issue 1,000,000 shares of stock. The initial street address of Acme, Inc.'s principal office is 123 Main St, San Francisco, CA 94103. The name of Acme, Inc.'s initial agent for service of process in California is Jordan Lee. The agent's street address in California is 123 Main St, San Francisco, CA 94103.

THE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF A CLOSE CORPORATION
California's General Corporation Law treats "close corporation" status as an election available within the ordinary corporate form, not a separate type of entity. A corporation qualifies as a close corporation only if its articles of incorporation contain two things beyond the content every corporation's articles must already include under Section 202: a provision capping the number of persons who may hold record ownership of all of the corporation's issued shares of all classes at a specific number the corporation chooses, which cannot exceed 35, and the literal statement "This corporation is a close corporation." Separately, a corporation's name must contain the word "corporation," "incorporated," or "limited" (or an abbreviation of one of those words) in order for the corporation to be subject to the General Corporation Law's close-corporation provisions at all — a naming requirement that does not apply to corporations generally.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Close corporation” means a corporation, including a close social purpose corporation, whose articles contain, in addition to the provisions required by Section 202, a provision that all of the corporation’s issued shares of all classes shall be held of record by not more than a specified number of persons, not exceeding 35, and a statement, “This corporation is a close corporation.”"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 158(a), California General Corporation Law, the definition of a close corporation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=158.)
  "The name of the corporation; provided, however, that in order for the corporation to be subject to the provisions of this division applicable to a close corporation (Section 158), the name of the corporation must contain the word “corporation,” “incorporated,” or “limited” or an abbreviation of one of such words."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 202(a), California General Corporation Law, the close-corporation name designator requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=202.)
  Known gap: This is one state's election mechanism within one state's general corporation statute, used as real evidence of what qualifies a specific corporation for status as a "close corporation" under California law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, or that other states offer an equivalent election at all; some states have no statutory close-corporation supplement to their general corporation law, and among those that do, the qualifying shareholder cap and required election language vary. The two citations below come from two independently enacted sections of the General Corporation Law: Cal. Corp. Code § 158(a) is the source of the definition itself, and Cal. Corp. Code § 202(a) is an independently verified second source for the corporate-name designator requirement that the close-corporation election specifically triggers.

ADDING OR REMOVING THE CLOSE CORPORATION ELECTION AFTER INCORPORATION
The close-corporation provision described above does not have to be included in a corporation's original articles of incorporation; California's statute lets a corporation add it later by amending its articles. But the vote required to make that change depends on timing. If the amendment adding the close-corporation provision is adopted after the corporation has already issued shares, it takes the affirmative vote of all of the corporation's issued and outstanding shares of every class — unanimous shareholder approval, not merely a majority. Removing the provision, or changing the specific shareholder-number cap once it is in the articles, works differently: if that amendment is likewise adopted after shares have been issued, the default rule requires the affirmative vote of at least two-thirds of the outstanding shares of each class, though the articles themselves may set a lower threshold (down to, but not below, a majority of the outstanding shares) or may deny a vote entirely to any particular class.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The special provisions referred to in subdivision (a) may be included in the articles by amendment, but if such amendment is adopted after the issuance of shares only by the affirmative vote of all of the issued and outstanding shares of all classes."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 158(b), California General Corporation Law, adding the close-corporation election by amendment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=158.)
  "The special provisions referred to in subdivision (a) may be deleted from the articles by amendment, or the number of shareholders specified may be changed by amendment, but if such amendment is adopted after the issuance of shares, only by the affirmative vote of at least two-thirds of each class of the outstanding shares; provided, however, that the articles may provide for a lesser vote, but not less than a majority of the outstanding shares, or may deny a vote to any class, or both."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 158(c), California General Corporation Law, removing or changing the election by amendment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=158.)
  Known gap: This is one state's amendment-voting mechanics for a specific statutory election, used as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a given corporation, and not a claim that every state offering an equivalent election requires the same voting thresholds. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 158(b) and § 158(c), so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones; no additional independent source was located for these amendment-vote thresholds specifically.

THE REQUIRED SHARE CERTIFICATE LEGEND AND THE CONSEQUENCE OF EXCEEDING THE CAP
Close corporation status carries its own certificate-disclosure requirement, separate from and stricter than the general share-transfer-restriction disclosure that applies to any California corporation's shares. Every certificate representing shares of a close corporation must carry a specific, conspicuous legend on its face stating that the corporation is a close corporation, naming the maximum number of holders of record its shares of all classes may have (a number not exceeding 35), and warning that any attempted voluntary inter vivos transfer that would violate that cap is void. That warning is not merely disclosure: if the certificate carries the required legend, an attempted voluntary transfer that would push the number of record holders of the corporation's shares past the maximum stated in the articles is void by statute, not just unenforceable against an unknowing transferee. Separately, the statute treats a shareholder's acceptance of a certificate bearing that legend as the shareholder's own consent to the restriction — including a waiver of any right the shareholder might otherwise have to sell to a broader pool of purchasers or to demand registration of the shares under federal securities law, for as long as the corporation remains a close corporation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "All certificates representing shares of a close corporation shall contain in addition to any other statements required by this section, the following conspicuous legend on the face thereof: “This corporation is a close corporation. The number of holders of record of its shares of all classes cannot exceed ____ [a number not in excess of 35]. Any attempted voluntary inter vivos transfer which would violate this requirement is void. Refer to the articles, bylaws and any agreements on file with the secretary of the corporation for further restrictions.”"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 418(c), California General Corporation Law, the required close-corporation certificate legend (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=418.)
  "Any attempted voluntary inter vivos transfer of the shares of a close corporation which would result in the number of holders of record of its shares exceeding the maximum number specified in its articles is void if the certificate contains the legend required by subdivision (c)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 418(d), California General Corporation Law, a transfer past the cap is void (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=418.)
  "Each holder of shares of a close corporation, whether original or subsequent, by accepting the certificates for the shares which contain the legend required by subdivision (c) of Section 418 agrees and consents that such holder cannot make any transfer of shares which would violate the provisions of subdivision (d) of Section 418 and waives any right which such holder might otherwise have under any other law to sell such shares to a greater number of purchasers or to demand any registration thereof under the Securities Act of 1933"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 421, California General Corporation Law, a shareholder's consent to the legend by accepting the certificate (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=421.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement specific to a corporate subtype that has elected close-corporation status — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and it applies only if that election was actually made, which most small corporations have not done. This project's Buy-Sell Agreement document separately covers Cal. Corp. Code § 418(c) and (d) for a different purpose — what a departing close-corporation shareholder's transfer restriction means for a buy-sell counterparty; this clause covers the same statutory legend requirement from the formation side, as something the articles and share certificates must build in from the outset. The § 418 citations below are both subsections of the same statutory section and are treated as one source; Cal. Corp. Code § 421 is an independently enacted second source confirming the consent-and-waiver consequence that attaches to accepting a legended certificate.

SHAREHOLDER MANAGEMENT AGREEMENTS IN PLACE OF A BOARD
The central practical feature of close corporation status is a statutory exception to the rule that a corporation's business and affairs must be managed by or under the direction of a board of directors. California's statute allows the shareholders of a close corporation to enter into a written shareholders' agreement — by definition, one signed by all of the corporation's shareholders — that governs any phase of the corporation's affairs, including management of its business, division of profits, or distribution of assets on liquidation. Such an agreement is not invalid merely because it interferes with the board's ordinary discretion or because it treats the corporation as if it were a partnership; the statute expressly protects an agreement of this kind from that objection. There are limits: the agreement cannot alter or waive certain other listed provisions of the General Corporation Law, and to the extent the agreement transfers the board's managerial discretion to particular shareholders, those shareholders take on the liability a director would otherwise bear for the same managerial acts, while the directors are relieved of that liability to the same extent. The statute also specifically provides that failing to observe ordinary corporate formalities around director or shareholder meetings, when that failure results from following such an agreement, is not by itself a factor supporting personal liability for the corporation's obligations.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "no shareholders’ agreement, which relates to any phase of the affairs of a close corporation, including but not limited to management of its business, division of its profits or distribution of its assets on liquidation, shall be invalid as between the parties thereto on the ground that it so relates to the conduct of the affairs of the corporation as to interfere with the discretion of the board or that it is an attempt to treat the corporation as if it were a partnership or to arrange their relationships in a manner that would be appropriate only between partners."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 300(b), California General Corporation Law, a close corporation shareholders' agreement is not invalid for displacing board discretion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=300.)
  "An agreement of the type referred to in subdivision (b) shall, to the extent and so long as the discretion or powers of the board in its management of corporate affairs is controlled by such agreement, impose upon each shareholder who is a party thereto liability for managerial acts performed or omitted by such person pursuant thereto that is otherwise imposed by this division upon directors, and the directors shall be relieved to that extent from such liability."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 300(d), California General Corporation Law, managing shareholders take on director-level liability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=300.)
  "The failure of a close corporation to observe corporate formalities relating to meetings of directors or shareholders in connection with the management of its affairs, pursuant to an agreement authorized by subdivision (b), shall not be considered a factor tending to establish that the shareholders have personal liability for corporate obligations."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 300(e), California General Corporation Law, relaxed corporate formalities under such an agreement are not evidence of personal liability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=300.)
  "“Shareholders’ agreement” means a written agreement among all of the shareholders of a close corporation, or if a close corporation has only one shareholder between such shareholder and the corporation, as authorized by subdivision (b) of Section 300."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 186, California General Corporation Law, the definition of a close corporation shareholders' agreement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=186.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutory basis for shareholders replacing board governance with a private agreement, used as real evidence that such a mechanism exists in at least one state's close-corporation law — not a claim about which state's law governs a given corporation, and the scope of any equivalent mechanism (and whether one exists at all) varies by state. Cal. Corp. Code § 300(b), (d), and (e) are subsections of one statutory section and are treated as one source; Cal. Corp. Code § 186, which supplies the statutory definition of a "shareholders' agreement" and cross-references § 300(b) directly, is an independently enacted second source. This clause does not itemize the specific other General Corporation Law provisions such an agreement cannot alter or waive; Section 300(c) lists them and was reviewed as part of this verification, but its list was not reproduced quote-by-quote here.

EXPANDED STANDING FOR CLOSE-CORPORATION SHAREHOLDERS IN DEADLOCK AND DISSOLUTION
California's involuntary-dissolution statute ordinarily limits who may file a court action to dissolve a corporation to specific, defined groups — among them, half or more of the sitting directors, or shareholders who together hold at least one-third of the corporation's outstanding shares. Close corporation status changes that threshold: the same statute separately grants standing to file for involuntary dissolution to any shareholder or shareholders of a close corporation, without regard to what percentage of the shares that shareholder holds. A parallel expansion applies to a related but distinct proceeding — asking a court to take jurisdiction over a corporation's voluntary winding up — where the statute again grants standing to any close-corporation shareholder, alongside the corporation itself, holders of five percent or more of a class of shares, and creditors. Separately, and not limited to formally-elected close corporations specifically, the same involuntary-dissolution statute lists a further ground available to any corporation with 35 or fewer shareholders: dissolution on the basis that liquidation is reasonably necessary to protect the complaining shareholder's rights or interests, without requiring the fraud, mismanagement, or board deadlock that the statute's other grounds demand. By contrast, California's court-appointed "provisional director" remedy for a deadlocked board or a deadlocked shareholder vote is a general corporate remedy available to any California corporation meeting its own conditions — it is not one of the sections the close-corporation definition itself identifies as containing close-corporation-specific provisions.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A shareholder or shareholders who hold shares representing not less than 33 1 / 3 percent of (i) the total number of outstanding shares (assuming conversion of any preferred shares convertible into common shares) or (ii) the outstanding common shares or (iii) the equity of the corporation, exclusive in each case of shares owned by persons who have personally participated in any of the transactions enumerated in paragraph (4) of subdivision (b), or any shareholder or shareholders of a close corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a)(2), California General Corporation Law, standing to petition for involuntary dissolution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1800.)
  "In the case of any corporation with 35 or fewer shareholders (determined as provided in Section 605), liquidation is reasonably necessary for the protection of the rights or interests of the complaining shareholder or shareholders."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(b)(5), California General Corporation Law, the 35-or-fewer-shareholder involuntary dissolution ground (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1800.)
  "upon the petition of (a) the corporation, or (b) a shareholder or shareholders who hold shares representing 5 percent or more of the total number of any class of outstanding shares, or (c) any shareholder or shareholders of a close corporation, or (d) three or more creditors"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1904, California General Corporation Law, standing to petition for court supervision of a voluntary winding up (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1904.)
  "If a corporation has an even number of directors who are equally divided and cannot agree as to the management of its affairs, so that its business can no longer be conducted to advantage or so that there is danger that its property and business will be impaired or lost, the superior court of the proper county may, notwithstanding any provisions of the articles or bylaws and whether or not an action is pending for an involuntary winding up or dissolution of the corporation, appoint a provisional director pursuant to this section."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 308(a), California General Corporation Law, the provisional-director remedy is a general corporate remedy, not close-corporation-specific (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=308.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that at least one state's close-corporation law expands standing to sue for involuntary dissolution or court supervision of winding up, and as evidence that a separate, nearby remedy (the provisional-director statute) is not itself limited to close corporations — not a claim about which state's law governs a given corporation, and not a claim that dissolution, winding-up supervision, or a provisional-director petition is warranted for any specific corporation. This clause corrects an assumption worth stating plainly: Cal. Corp. Code § 158(g), the close-corporation definition section, lists the specific sections it identifies as containing close-corporation-specific provisions (Sections 186, 202, 204, 300, 418, 421, 1111, 1201, 1800, and 1904), and Section 308, the provisional-director statute, is not among them — that remedy exists for any corporation with an even-numbered deadlocked board or a deadlocked shareholder vote, not as a feature exclusive to close corporations. Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a)(2) and § 1800(b)(5) are subsections of one statutory section and are treated as one source; Cal. Corp. Code § 1904 is an independently enacted second source; Cal. Corp. Code § 308 is cited here specifically to support the corrective point that it is a general remedy, not a close-corporation-specific one.

CLOSE CORPORATION INCORPORATOR SIGNATURE
Executed by the incorporator:

Incorporator: Jordan Alex Lee

Signature: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, standing to petition for court supervision of a voluntary winding up
citations.quote: upon the petition of (a) the corporation, or (b) a shareholder or shareholders who hold shares representing 5 percent or more of the total number of any class of outstanding shares, or (c) any shareholder or shareholders of a close corporation, or (d) three or more creditors

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the provisional-director remedy is a general corporate remedy, not close-corporation-specific
citations.quote: If a corporation has an even number of directors who are equally divided and cannot agree as to the management of its affairs, so that its business can no longer be conducted to advantage or so that there is danger that its property and business will be impaired or lost, the superior court of the proper county may, notwithstanding any provisions of the articles or bylaws and whether or not an action is pending for an involuntary winding up or dissolution of the corporation, appoint a provisional director pursuant to this section.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that at least one state's close-corporation law expands standing to sue for involuntary dissolution or court supervision of winding up, and as evidence that a separate, nearby remedy (the provisional-director statute) is not itself limited to close corporations — not a claim about which state's law governs a given corporation, and not a claim that dissolution, winding-up supervision, or a provisional-director petition is warranted for any specific corporation. This clause corrects an assumption worth stating plainly: Cal. Corp. Code § 158(g), the close-corporation definition section, lists the specific sections it identifies as containing close-corporation-specific provisions (Sections 186, 202, 204, 300, 418, 421, 1111, 1201, 1800, and 1904), and Section 308, the provisional-director statute, is not among them — that remedy exists for any corporation with an even-numbered deadlocked board or a deadlocked shareholder vote, not as a feature exclusive to close corporations. Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a)(2) and § 1800(b)(5) are subsections of one statutory section and are treated as one source; Cal. Corp. Code § 1904 is an independently enacted second source; Cal. Corp. Code § 308 is cited here specifically to support the corrective point that it is a general remedy, not a close-corporation-specific one.
